Forgotten World - Mpumalanga Stone Terraces

By: Jane Lipman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Over 500 years ago a complex African farming system existed in Mpumalanga and yet its not known and not a heritage site ..why?

Summary:
New discoveries in the last ten years show that on the beautiful escarpments of Mpumalanga are stone circles showing proof of complex African cattle homesteads that existed 600 years ago . The aerial views show dramatic pictures of an ancient forgotten civilisation and archaelogists have evidence of complex trading systems and lifestyles . Yet the site , on the road from Johannesburg to the Kruger Park ,is not a heritage site and rubbish lies in places that should be honoured and preserved . We ask the government why ?

Expert:
Mr. Peter Delius
Ms. Alex Schoeman
Mr. Sandile Memela

Mpumalanga

Press Release:


Forgotten World
One of the most remarkable archaeological and historical heritage sites on the subcontinent, Bokoni covers 10 000 square kilometres of the Mpumalanga escarpment. Yet despite its size, significance and astonishing beauty, it has remained a forgotten world, ignored by scholars, tourism and heritage agencies. Carte Blanche visits the site of remarkable formations that evidence massive human settlement before colonialism.


Script:


SCRIPT FORGOTTEN WORLD
VOICE OVER IN RED

In Mpumalanga , known as “the place where the sun rises “ and as a province of great geographical diversity and beauty there is an ancient place shown by the engravings and stone walls amongst the soaring escarpment and rolling hills.
Link Claire
Here in Bokoni an area which covers 10, 000 square kilometres in Mpumalanga lies a remarkable archaeological and historical site that remains forgotten. As many 100,000 people lived here in the 18 th century feeding into trading systems that stretched as far as the Indian Ocean

Sound Up Thabang Makwetla
Those stone walls it was a mystic discovery that I was eager to know and understand .

Sound up Peter Delius

They have been under researched and more or less ignored by historians and more or less ignored by the Heritage authorities .
But Pedi people always knew of Bokoni and historian Peter Delius and Archaeologist Alex Schoeman have been studying their historic world for the last decade .
Peter “the sites are not protected , some of them are on private land and at the mercy effectively of land owners , many of them are under commercial forest , some of them are in areas of major road development so you have this extraordinary spread of sites across this vast area , they really at the mercy of pretty much what ever people want to do to them.
Stand up Claire “Here is one of many thousands of significant sites on the Mpumalanga escarpment located right on the N4 it is unprotected and unrecognised as an official heritage site

Despite Bokoni’s historical significance , the Ministry of Arts and Culture surprisingly have no preservation plan in place and were not aware of the site until they saw the Wits University research last week .



Sound up Minister
That is why the study by Wits of what happened in Mpumalanga , the Makoni , becomes very important , we should continue doing that because we should be in a position to discover and rediscover ourselves so much has not been said and been discovered about Africa and South Africa in particular .


The sites were built by Africans as early as the sixteenth century , and show built stone structures, in contrast to the conventional wisdom about how Africans farmed in pre colonial times . The settlements stretch from Carolina to Ohrigstad near Nelspruit and beyond .The communities lived here from 1500 to the 1820’s . This world was caught up in the emergence of powerful African states , as well as new trading and farming systems .

Sound up Peter Delius Historian
It’s a society that develops a remarkable system of intensive farming and draws in people from all around and all of those people together create a new world and a new culture .

The people from many different groups ,creating this new culture became known as BaKoni , they had come from Kwa Zulu Natal and surrounding areas .Their farming techniques using regular terraces and fertilizer , formed part of the biggest intensive pre colonial farming system in Southern and Eastern Africa .
Thabang Makwetla comes from the area .
Sound up Thabang Makwetla
My father had a few cattle , I think I remember , three or four, which forced me to be looking after cattle and up there and across the river , where it was grazing land , you find stone walls , that technique of building a stone wall , I learnt to do it myself as a youngster . Now and again the cattle would jump over the thing , the wall would fall , I must go there and like you know build it , so I knew exactly the technique of playing around with ordering of these stones such that the structure remains intact .


Sound up Alex
We can see many things from the stone walls , and we can see the extent of this area ,we can trace the scale of Bokoni from Ohrighstad to Carolina ,we can trace the scale of some of the towns such as Kutwaneng and we can see through the roads in these towns that all the roads were connected so this is an interconnected village not just home steads .

In the daily routine of the Koni the women would fetch water from one of the many local rivers, farm and prepare food for the day while the boys and men would herd cattle and maintain stone walls .

Alex sound up
So for example its womens daily working in the garden that shaped the terraces , that she planted the food in the terraces that we see today , its womens daily actions in the domestic space that configured those spaces and shaped them in the way that we see today .
Claire stand up “This Bokoni settlement is a stone wall circular structure that housed the cattle on the inside and the households along the outside , built in shale African farmers spent years consolidating their home stead showing their dedication to this land


Question from Claire “We know a lot about other groups , the Xhosa , the Zulu , the Pedi ,but we don’t know much about the people who lived there , who are they and where did they come from ?”
Answer Peter Delius
These are groups who came from a variety of different places, probably quite a significant ..moving from low lying areas and moving out of Kwa Zulu Natal , who move in to this area , settle there and start to evolve this really fascinating intensive farming system and society .
The Bakoni left many clues of their world , there are prolific engravings that have been found near Lydenburg . These are representations of the way they lived .
There are not many iron smelting sites in the area , suggesting that iron was being imported . A large iron hoe was used in the rocky ground for cultivating .
These are communities that invested vast quantities of energy and effort and skill into their farming activities over a very long period of time . They also weren’t isolated , they were much more widely connected ,they were connected to regional trading systems in iron and copper and other goods which spanned the Northern Transvaal to the Eastern Cape and they were part of trading networks that linked to the east coast and the much wider ancient Eastern trading world.



Stand up Claire
The peace loving Bokoni were driven out of this area by militarized branches of the Ndebele and Ndwandwe .
As the eighteenth century goes by we see the emergence in South Africa of more highly militarized societies that are much more aggressive in their activities and devote more time to military training and military technology.
Bokoni societies were poorly equipped because they were focussed on the logic of production , and couldn’t deal with groups driven by the logic of raiding and warfare .


The Bakoni retreated into the deep gorges found in the escarpment , but they couldn’t survive in those gorges .
By the early 1800’s , the Swazi , the Ndebele and the Ndwandwe were raiding into the Escarpment , taking the cattle, the grain and the women and children . Today the descendents of the Bakoni are scattered particularly in the Pedi kingdom.

Now parts of the area are abandoned and this critical part of South African history is left to vandals and litter .Alex Schoeman says the public need access to these sites in a regulated way .

Alex sound up
What we know now is that site conservation and accessibility goes hand in hand , so when sites are accessible and tourists can access them , can learn about these societies and how they function , people care more , and that caring translates into more effective conservation .
Peter Delius sound up
It seems to me theres an extraordinary opportunity here to develop sections of these sites to train people in their significance to allow craft and other industries to develop around them so that we can actually create some thing of a local economy around these sites .


Minister We believe that we should do everything in our power , want to raise consciousness within our society



Sound up Peter Delius
Unfortunately these sites have not been preserved that have not been recognised , they have not been listed , this despite the fact that over the last ten years or more we have done a huge amount to try to raise public consciousness of these sites and briefed a whole range of different politicians and national provincial government about it so theres certainly been some support particularly from the premier of Mpumalanga Thabang Makwetla , but other than that there has been very little effort to preserve these sites for future generations .
Thabang Makwetla sound up
As government , much must be done to provide the necessary support to bring this place back to life .


Minister sound up
When such has been discovered as in Mpumalanga , what do we do to preserve that ? What do you do to promote that ? Because we want , when we say we want to uplift this section of the portfolio which is heritage , we are not saying that we want it to overshadow arts and culture , but we are saying that people must know its there , and those things which need to be preserved are preserved and promoted to the public , their significance so that everybody becomes part of owning our common heritage …
